quote: Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?
source: Thornton Wilder, Our Town, Act III, the graveyard scene (Emily)
speaker: Emily
note: Corrected: the proposal named the speaker twice and called her Emily Webb, her maiden name, though in Act III she is married to George Gibbs. No edition of the play was opened. The question mark after it is Wilder's own, printed before a dash, on the agreement of eight published books quoting the passage.

evidence.where: The refutation's charge was that the card's terminal question mark might be minted, because the printed sentence runs on past it. That is now answered against the refutation. A full-text search of scanned printed books through Open Library returns eight independently typeset volumes quoting the passage, and they agree character for character that Wilder prints a question mark after it, then a dash, then every, every minute? They are Readings on Our Town (Greenhaven), Readings on Thornton Wilder (ed. Katie De Koster), Mary Ellen Snodgrass, Our Town: notes, Quintessential Pleasures (Metropolitan Museum of Art), James B. Dunning, Ministries, Sharing God's Gifts, Robert L. Randall, Walking Through the Valley, Gregory A. Boyd, Present Perfect, and Harry E. Moore, Profiles. Readings on Our Town also quotes the sentence truncated exactly where this card truncates it, stopping at live it?, which shows the stop is an accepted quotation boundary and not an invention. The three renderings the refutation relied on that lack the question mark are all retyped theatre working documents and are demonstrably unreliable: the Improv Playhouse audition sides, a 68 page web script transcription that substitutes an ellipsis for every dash in the speech, and the Shea's Performing Arts monologue handout, which converts several of the speech's commas into question marks. The Goodreads Does anyone ever realize life variant is a third party misquotation and is contradicted by all eight printed books. Attribution, play, act, scene and speaker were never in doubt: Emily asks it of the Stage Manager after reliving her twelfth birthday, and he answers No, then the saints and poets, maybe. shipped.js returns nothing shipped and nothing near; Wilder stands at one for the year from the February Bridge of San Luis Rey line, under the cap of three, not banned, and appears once in June. In scope: a play first published 1938. No content warning needed. The source line is 63 characters, leads with the author's name, carries no dash and no straight double quote. The remaining gap is procedural rather than substantive: no copy of the play itself was opened, so the wording rests on printed books quoting it rather than on the play's own page, and the note says so.
evidence.edition: No edition of Our Town opened. Wording corroborated in eight scanned published books quoting the passage, chiefly Readings on Our Town (Greenhaven Press) and Mary Ellen Snodgrass, Our Town: notes.
evidence.locator: Act III, the graveyard scene, Emily to the Stage Manager after reliving her twelfth birthday

reason: The refutation was right that the earlier pass had not earned its confidence, and right that the empty note would have shipped the doubt invisibly. Both faults are now repaired. Eight independently typeset printed books agree that Wilder prints the question mark after it, which is stronger evidence of the edition's punctuation than one transcriber's copy would be, and the sources that lack it are retyped theatre documents that normalise punctuation elsewhere in the same speech. The locator is corrected: the old line named the speaker twice and used her maiden name. The line does not fail twice, so it is not a REJECT, and the attribution is certain, so an Attributed to hedge would misdirect the doubt onto the one thing nobody disputes. It ships corrected, with the provenance stated plainly.
